article.overview: A lidar scanner is an active imaging sensor. It sends out laser light, measures how long the light takes to return or how its frequency has shifted, and uses those measurements to build a set of three-dimensional surface points. Compared with a camera, it produces distances directly, so it can map terrain and detect hazards in darkness and under low-angle sunlight, where image-based methods are weaker. In scope: lidar systems that build a 2D or 3D surface map from many range measurements, including scanning (beam-steered) lidars, flash lidars that record a full range image per pulse, and FMCW coherent lidars that build point clouds. Out of scope, with cross-references: single-spot or profiling altimeters (047 Laser altimeter); single-beam rangefinders (048 Laser rangefinder); Doppler lidar for velocity and landing navigation, such as the Navigation Doppler Lidar flown on Intuitive Machines IM-1 (179 Doppler lidar); camera-based hazard detection (031 Hazard detection camera); stereo-image terrain mapping (028 Terrain mapping camera); and gridded topographic and orbital topography products (050 Digital terrain mapping system and 051 Surface topography mapper). The examples have different statuses. The Chang'e-3 obstacle-avoidance lidar is the only example described in the sources accessed as flown on a lunar mission. The ALHAT Flash Lidar was flight-tested on an Earth-based lander in a lunar-like hazard field. The NASA Langley Terrain Sensing Lidar has been flight-tested on drones and helicopters. KNaCK is a prototype. Moonraker is a proposed ESA-studied orbital lidar mapper. No example other than the Chang'e-3 sensor is verified as flying a lidar scanner to the Moon.
article.description: A lidar, from light detection and ranging, measures distance with a laser. A scanner repeats these measurements over a surface and combines them into a map. Three design choices matter. First, how the beam covers the scene: a scanning lidar steers one beam or a small group of beams with mirrors, as in the Chang'e-3 sensor, which uses two galvanometer mirrors and 16 beams; a flash lidar lights the whole scene with one pulse and records a range for each pixel of a detector array, giving a complete 3D frame per pulse. Second, how range is measured: a pulsed lidar times the round trip of each pulse; an FMCW lidar sends a continuously frequency-modulated beam and compares the return with the transmitted signal, giving range and, through the Doppler shift, the velocity of the surface relative to the sensor. The KNaCK record describes a velocity-sensing coherent FMCW lidar that records Doppler velocity at each sampled range point. Third, the output: a point cloud, a range image or a digital elevation model, each useful for hazard analysis, navigation or topographic mapping but needing its own accuracy and resolution.
article.scientific_purpose_and_applications: Landing-hazard detection and safe-site selection: the Chang'e-3 sensor was used during the hovering phase to build 3D terrain of the landing area and detect small hazards such as rocks or potholes. The ALHAT Flash Lidar was used in flight to scan a lunar-like hazard field, build a digital elevation map and select a safe landing site. The NASA Langley Terrain Sensing Lidar is designed for hazard detection and avoidance during landing. Navigation without GPS: the KNaCK system is intended for mapping and navigation where GPS is unavailable, building terrain point clouds while measuring Doppler velocity to support a six-degree-of-freedom pose estimate. Mapping of shadowed or low-light terrain: the KNaCK abstract says image-based robotic navigation struggles under the extremely low-angle sunlight at the lunar South Pole, and that a lidar-based method does not depend on imagery; ESA's Moonraker study lists scanning permanently shadowed regions for water ice among its science goals. Topographic mapping from orbit: the Moonraker concept would produce wide-area elevation maps of the polar regions and higher-resolution scans of specific landing sites. Its design values are not verified in this article.
article.operating_principle: Lidar ranging relies on the travel time of light: distance equals half the round-trip time multiplied by the speed of light. Scanning pulsed lidar (Chang'e-3 example): a pulsed laser is split into 16 beams by a grating and steered by two galvanometer mirrors mounted perpendicular to each other. The returned light is received in parallel by a multi-channel detector, and a timing circuit provides the range for each channel. Figure 1 shows the scanning arrangement with the scanning mirror (X) and pointing mirror (Y). Flash lidar (ALHAT and Terrain Sensing Lidar): one broad laser pulse is emitted and the return is recorded on a detector array, so each pixel gives a range. The NASA Langley record describes the Terrain Sensing Lidar as a linear-mode flash lidar sensor. FMCW coherent lidar (KNaCK): the laser frequency is modulated; the frequency difference between outgoing and returned light gives range, and the Doppler shift gives radial velocity.
article.scientific_importance: Lidar scanners give direct distance measurements, which allows terrain to be mapped in three dimensions without depending on sunlight. For landers this matters for hazard detection. The ALHAT flight tests identified landing hazards as small as 30 cm from a maximum slant range of 450 m. The Chang'e-3 sensor was designed to detect small obstacles during hovering. These results show that lidar hazard detection can work in flight, but they do not show the same performance in every lunar lighting, dust or surface condition. For mapping, a lidar gives an absolute elevation measurement that a camera alone does not; Moonraker's science and site-survey goals and KNaCK's proposed navigation method both depend on this. Lidar data complement imagery: lidar gives geometry, cameras give texture and colour. Cross-references: 028 for stereo imaging and 031 for camera-based hazard detection.

physical_specifications.note: There is no universal specification for a lidar scanner. The examples use different laser approaches, mounting arrangements and mission roles, and the sources accessed publish only a few values for each. Where a value is not published it is recorded as 'not publicly specified'. Values are tied to the named example and are not meant to rank the examples. The comparison table in the Markdown article is not like-for-like: the columns describe different instruments, documents and maturity levels. The Chang'e-3 accuracy is a post-calibration 3D surface accuracy; the ALHAT value is a flight-test range precision and accuracy; the TSL and KNaCK have no published numerical performance in the sources accessed.

physical_specifications.dimensions_and_proportions: No verified dimensions are recorded for any lidar scanner in this article, except the Chang'e-3 laser exit window (about 120 mm wide) and the rough form factor of KNaCK (backpack-mounted). The sensor's dimensions must be set by its field of view, beam count, optics, thermal control and mounting interface. For a scanning lidar, the exit window and the mirror swing (plus or minus 15 degrees for the Chang'e-3 sensor) determine part of the envelope. A new design would need its dimensions set by its intended mission, not by these examples.
physical_specifications.mass_and_weight: No mass is publicly specified for any of the lidar scanners in the sources accessed. Mass affects launch cost, lander capacity, structural support and deployment design, so it should be taken from a verified instrument specification for any named mission. The article does not infer mass from the examples.
physical_specifications.power_requirements: No power figure is publicly specified for the Chang'e-3, ALHAT, TSL, KNaCK or Moonraker examples in the sources accessed. Lidar power depends on pulse energy, repetition rate, detector cooling, scanning mechanism and processing, so the absence of a figure should not be read as zero power.

article.environmental_and_operational_requiremen: Lidar scanners operate in vacuum and under strong thermal cycling, like other lunar surface and orbital instruments. Three specific operational concerns are recorded in the sources. Dust and exhaust: the ALHAT flight test showed that rocket-engine heat caused scintillation and that a dust cloud raised during launch could pre-trigger the sensor under some wind conditions; a lunar lander's plume and dust are likely to be a similar concern, but the sources accessed do not test this on the Moon. Lighting: KNaCK's abstract describes image-based navigation as difficult under very low sun angles at the South Pole; a lidar uses its own illumination, but the sources accessed give no lunar performance figure for it. Calibration and alignment: the Chang'e-3 calibration work shows that a scanning lidar needs careful calibration to reach a usable accuracy. Uncalibrated errors could produce a false obstacle about 1.4 m high, and calibration brought the 3D surface accuracy to about 4 cm. The sensor's position and attitude must be known relative to the ground frame, which the paper handled with a calibration structure and target plates.
article.limitations: A lidar scanner measures distance to the surface it illuminates. It does not measure composition, and it gives no reflectance information unless wavelength and return intensity are used in a specific way. Its output depends on the laser return from the surface, so dark, dusty or specular surfaces can give weaker returns. Resolution is limited by beam or pixel size, sensor range, scan rate and pose knowledge. The examples are not comparable as one product: the Chang'e-3 values come from a 2022 calibration paper about a flown instrument; the ALHAT values come from a conference paper about Earth-based flight tests; the TSL and KNaCK have very little published performance data; Moonraker is a proposal. The article does not claim that any example other than the Chang'e-3 sensor has flown to the Moon.

transportation_and_deployment.overview: Lidar scanners can be carried as a lander payload, a rover or crew-carried system, or an orbiter instrument. Only the Chang'e-3 sensor is documented as flown on a lunar lander. The other examples were flown on Earth-based vehicles or aircraft, are prototypes, or are proposals, so their lunar transport and deployment interfaces are not verified.
transportation_process: Integrate the lidar into the lander, rover or spacecraft payload on Earth, with a defined mounting interface and calibrated alignment to the vehicle frame.
Launch and transfer to the Moon (for orbital concepts such as Moonraker, orbit insertion and commissioning would follow).
For lander-mounted hazard lidars, operate during the descent or hovering phase, as the Chang'e-3 sensor did, with its scan used to map the landing area.

For a crew-carried or rover-carried mapping system such as KNaCK, mount the sensor on a backpack or rover and operate it during traverse; this is a described form factor and intended use, not a verified lunar deployment.
For orbital mapping, downlink lidar data to Earth and process it into digital elevation models (reported for Moonraker in secondary summaries; not verified).
transportation_and_deployment.deployment_methods: Chang'e-3: the lidar was part of the lander payload and used during the hovering phase [1]. ALHAT and TSL: flight-tested as descent or aircraft sensors, not deployed on the Moon [2][3]. KNaCK: backpack-mounted prototype; crew or rover mounting is the intended use [4]. Moonraker: spacecraft-mounted orbital concept; the spacecraft bus, orbit insertion and data downlink would need study-level definition [5][6].
transportation_and_deployment.historical_examples: The Chang'e-3 obstacle-avoidance lidar is the best-documented flown lunar-surface scanner in this article. The ALHAT flight tests on the Morpheus lander demonstrated flash-lidar hazard mapping and guided landing in flight, but on Earth. Apollo laser altimetry is covered in 047.
transportation_and_deployment.compatibility_assessment: No lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted in this article. Compatibility would require verified mass, dimensions, mounting points, power, data, thermal and field-of-view interface documents for the named vehicle and lidar. The Chang'e-3 lidar's use on its own lander is documented; compatibility with any other lander is not.

article.historical_significance: The Chang'e-3 obstacle-avoidance lidar is the best-documented flown lunar-surface scanner in this article. It was used during the lander's hovering phase to detect small hazards and build 3D terrain of the landing area. The ALHAT flight tests were a milestone for flash-lidar hazard detection, showing in flight that a lidar could map hazards and guide a vehicle to a selected site, although the tests were on Earth. The Terrain Sensing Lidar and KNaCK show the development of lidar systems for lunar landing and navigation. Moonraker is a current European study of an orbital lidar mapper. The altimetry and Doppler lidar lines of development are covered in 047 and 179, including the Navigation Doppler Lidar flown on IM-1.
article.limitations_and_uncertainties: Chang'e-3 wavelength, range, mass, power and dimensions are not stated in the paper accessed. The ALHAT wavelength, field of view, frame rate, 3D frame size, mass and power are not stated in the paper accessed. The ALHAT helicopter tests reported in earlier search summaries could not be confirmed and are not used. The Terrain Sensing Lidar full specification record was not accessible; only the abstract and metadata were read. KNaCK has no numerical specifications in its primary record, and its secondary-reported demonstrations are unverified. Moonraker's Phase A status and its orbit and ground sample distance values come from secondary summaries; the primary PDF and press release were not readable. The Chang'e-4 lidar, the Clementine imaging lidar and the Apollo laser altimetry details reported in secondary sources are not verified and are not used in the specifications. The article contains no lunar landing-site or location recommendation.

image_handling.url_policy: All image_url and source_page_url values in this file have query strings and fragments removed. Section-level image objects are repeated intentionally so each article section can render its own images without resolving IDs against the master gallery. The four images are Chang'e-3 figures from Wang et al. (2022) verified as direct files returning HTTP 200 (image/jpeg). The overview and transportation_and_deployment image arrays are intentionally empty because no verified image is shown in those sections of the article.

data_quality_notes: Chang'e-3 TDI lidar: laser wavelength, measurement range, mass, power and full dimensions are not stated in Wang et al. (2022); recorded as not publicly specified. The 2024 Remote Sensing review that is reported to cover the sensor's system design could not be accessed (HTTP 403).
Chang'e-3 landing date is not stated in the paper; only the 2 December 2013 launch date is recorded.

ALHAT Flash Lidar: wavelength, field of view, frame rate, 3D frame size, mass and power are not stated in Roback et al. (2016). Earlier search summaries reported helicopter flight tests with conflicting platform details; these are not used.
Terrain Sensing Lidar: only the NTRS abstract and metadata were read. The linked PDF could not be read, so no numerical specifications are recorded.

KNaCK: the primary NTRS record gives no numerical specifications. The drone demonstration, New Mexico backpack trial and soda-can-size future unit come from secondary press and search summaries and were not verified from primary NASA text.

Moonraker: the Phase A selection and the 50 km orbit, 4 m (1X) and 0.5 m (8X) ground sample distances are from secondary summaries. The SpaceOps 2025 PDF could not be read and the SatNow press page returned HTTP 403. The GPS World report (June 2025) confirms the study, partners and science goals only.

Chang'e-4 descent lidar, Clementine imaging lidar and Apollo laser altimetry details appear only in secondary sources (a news blog and a search summary) and are not verified or used in the specifications.

Images: four direct Chang'e-3 figure URLs from the PMC article were verified by HTTP 200 with image/jpeg content. Their credit lines and reuse licence were not verified in this run. No verified direct image was found for ALHAT flight-test photographs, the Terrain Sensing Lidar, KNaCK or Moonraker; no image URL was invented for them. The PMC article page is used as the source page, not an official agency page, so direct_image_assets_verified_from_official_pages is false.
Full-resolution image downloads were not checked; the verified files are the journal's web-resolution figure files.
Transportation compatibility: no lander, rover or spacecraft compatibility is asserted for any example. The Chang'e-3 lidar's use on its own lander is documented; no other compatibility is verified.

Scope boundaries: lidar scanners are distinguished from altimeters (047), rangefinders (048) and Doppler lidar (179). The Navigation Doppler Lidar on IM-1 is referenced only for context and is not described as a lidar scanner.
No lunar landing-site or location recommendation is included, as requested.
